newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia hails success in limiting cocoa pest.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia hails success in limiting cocoa pest.

text.p: Some Indonesian cocoa farmers may soon be able to boost their crops by up to 30 percent thanks to new pruning and harvesting techniques which limit pest damage, an industry official said on Thursday.
Tests on plots in South Sulawesi have had huge success in cutting down the presence of the dreaded pod borer moth, Halim Razak, vice-chairman of the Indonesia Cocoa Association, told Reuters.
"The results have been fantastic," he said.
The pest is considered a major threat to boosting cocoa output in Indonesia, the world's third largest producer after the Ivory Coast and Ghana.
The moth lays its eggs on the cocoa pod, the larvae penetrate the hard shell and feed on the kernel, the source of the world's chocolate.
Razak said crop loss due to the pest on five one-hectare (2.5 acre) test plots was a mere five percent compared with 30 to 35 percent in areas infested with the pod borer.
"This means crop yield in areas affected with the pod borer can increase by about 30 percent if farmers used the same techniques applied on the demonstration plots," he said.

The techniques were introduced by British entomologist John Mumford of London University's Imperial College and involve regular pruning of the cocoa tree, and regular, frequent and complete harvesting of cocoa pods.

The pruning creates an open canopy that can be penetrated by sunshine -- anathema to the pest -- while the regular harvesting prevents the larvae from developing into caterpillars and later into moths.
The experiments were carried out with help from the American Cocoa Research Institute in its first collaboration with the Indonesian Cocoa Association to battle the pest.
Razak said a report on the outcome of the experiment would be submitted to the government in a bid to get state help in encouraging widespread use of the new techniques.
He said the report would outline long-term measures the industry can take to tackle the problem, adding that the experiment would be carried out for three years.
"If farmers can use the simple methods we used in the demonstration plots, I see great potential in increasing Indonesia's cocoa production in the coming years," he said.
"We finally might have found the solution to the pod borer pest and it's now up to the farmer to implement the techniques and increase their output," he said.
Indonesia's cocoa production is estimated by the cocoa association at between 319,000 and 330,000 tonnes in 1997, up 10 percent from 1996. Output is expected to exceed 400,000 tonnes by 2000.
